[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Advanced TensorFlow: Custom Layers, Loss Functions, and Metrics"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"While TensorFlow's high-level API provides a rich set of pre-built components, real-world machine learning tasks often require bespoke architectures and optimization objectives. This tutorial demonstrates how to extend TensorFlow by implementing custom layers, loss functions, and metrics using the Keras functional and subclassing APIs."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Prerequisites and Setup"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Ensure you have TensorFlow installed in your environment. We will import the necessary modules from tensorflow and numpy."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras import layers, Model
import numpy as np

print("TensorFlow version:", tf.__version__)"},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Building a Custom Layer"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"To create a custom layer, you must subclass tf.keras.layers.Layer and implement three primary methods: __init__ (for layer state/weights), build (to know the input shapes and create weights), and call (to define the forward pass computation)."},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"class Linear(layers.Layer):
    def __init__(self, units=32):
        super(Linear, self).__init__()
        self.units = units

    def build(self, input_shape):
        self.w = self.add_weight(
            shape=(input_shape[-1], self.units),
            initializer="random_normal",
            trainable=True,
        )
        self.b = self.add_weight(
            shape=(self.units,),
            initializer="zeros",
            trainable=True,
        )

    def call(self, inputs):
        return tf.matmul(inputs, self.w) + self.b"},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Creating a Custom Loss Function"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Custom losses can be implemented as Python functions that accept y_true and y_pred as arguments. For stateful losses or losses requiring configuration parameters, it is recommended to subclass tf.keras.losses.Loss."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"class CustomMSE(tf.keras.losses.Loss):
    def __init__(self, regularization_factor=0.1, name="custom_mse"):
        super().__init__(name=name)
        self.regularization_factor = regularization_factor

    def call(self, y_true, y_pred):
        base_loss = tf.reduce_mean(tf.square(y_true - y_pred))
        # Adding an arbitrary penalty based on prediction magnitude
        penalty = self.regularization_factor * tf.reduce_mean(tf.abs(y_pred))
        return base_loss + penalty"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Developing Custom Metrics"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Unlike loss functions, metrics do not affect backpropagation; instead, they evaluate model performance. Subclass tf.keras.metrics.Metric and override __init__, update_state, and result methods to maintain running statistics."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"class CategoricalTruePositives(tf.keras.metrics.Metric):
    def __init__(self, name="categorical_true_positives", **kwargs):
        super(CategoricalTruePositives, self).__init__(name=name, **kwargs)
        self.true_positives = self.add_weight(name="tp", initializer="zeros")

    def update_state(self, y_true, y_pred, sample_weight=None):
        y_true = tf.cast(y_true, tf.bool)
        y_pred = tf.cast(y_pred, tf.bool)
        
        # Find where both are true
        values = tf.logical_and(y_true, y_pred)
        values = tf.cast(values, tf.float32)
        
        if sample_weight is not None:
            sample_weight = tf.cast(sample_weight, tf.float32)
            values = tf.multiply(values, sample_weight)
            
        self.true_positives.assign_add(tf.reduce_sum(values))

    def result(self):
        return self.true_positives

    def reset_state(self):
        self.true_positives.assign(0.0)"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"4. Integrating Custom Components in a Model"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"Now, let's assemble our custom layer, custom loss, and custom metric into a standard model training pipeline using model.compile() and model.fit()."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"# Generate dummy data
x_train = np.random.random((100, 10)).astype(np.float32)
y_train = np.random.random((100, 1)).astype(np.float32)

# Build a model using the custom Linear layer
inputs = layers.Input(shape=(10,))
x = Linear(16)(inputs)
x = layers.Activation("relu")(x)
outputs = Linear(1)(x)
model = Model(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs)

# Compile the model with our custom loss and metric
model.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss=CustomMSE(regularization_factor=0.05),
    metrics=[tf.keras.metrics.MeanAbsoluteError()]
)

# Train the model
history = model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=5, batch_size=32)"},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary and Best Practices"},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always implement the build method in custom layers to dynamically infer input shapes and instantiate weights securely."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use vectorized TensorFlow operations (like tf.reduce_mean and tf.square) in losses and metrics to ensure graph execution compatibility and high performance."},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Remember to implement reset_state within custom metrics to clear tracking variables between epochs."}]
